title: Sputnik 1, 1957 — the beep that frightened America
sources: Wikipedia: Sputnik 1 — first artificial Earth satellite, launched by the Soviet Union on 4 October 1957 from the Tyuratam range in the Kazakh SSR (now Baikonur); a polished metal sphere 58 cm in diameter with four antennas; each orbit took 96.2 minutes; a one-watt radio transmitter; its 'beep-beep-beep' tones; radio signal easily detectable by amateur radio operators, 'anyone possessing a short wave receiver can hear' it; sent a signal for three weeks before its three silver-zinc batteries were depleted; fell back on 4 January 1958 after 1,440 orbits; public reaction to the Sputnik crisis led to the creation of NASA and increased spending on research and education; two American physicists, William Guier and George Weiffenbach, monitored its radio transmissions and realised through the Doppler effect they could pinpoint where it was — the seeds of modern satellite navigation

Wikipedia: Sputnik crisis — a period of public fear and anxiety in Western nations; the same rocket that launched Sputnik could send a nuclear warhead anywhere in the world in a matter of minutes; the failure of the first two Project Vanguard launch attempts

Archive film (public domain, Wikimedia Commons): Universal-International newsreels '1957-10-07 New Moon' (incl. its animation of the launch and orbit, and satellite tracking by computer) and '1958-02-06 Vanguard Fails in Second Launching'

Photos (public domain / CC0): Sputnik 1 replica (NASA NSSDC; Smithsonian); exploded view of Sputnik 1 (Memorial Museum of Cosmonautics); Vanguard rocket explodes, 6 December 1957 (US Navy); Soviet stamp of 5 November 1957; Caltech yearbook cartoon, 1958

post.facebook:
On this day in 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite.

It was a polished metal sphere 58 centimetres across, with four antennas and a one-watt radio. It circled the Earth every 96 minutes, and anyone with a shortwave receiver could hear its beep-beep-beep.

In the West, it brought fear: the rocket that had carried it could also carry a nuclear warhead anywhere in the world within minutes. America's answer, the Vanguard rocket, failed on its first two attempts. Public alarm led to the creation of NASA and to more money for science and education.

Two American physicists, William Guier and George Weiffenbach, listened to Sputnik's signal and realised they could work out exactly where it was from the Doppler shift — the seed of modern satellite navigation.

Sputnik's batteries died after three weeks. It fell back into the atmosphere on 4 January 1958, after 1,440 orbits.
